hpi_details: 39F with 1-year history of moon facies, buffalo hump, violaceous abdominal striae, and proximal weakness. Elevated 24h urinary cortisol.
ideas: She thinks her dramatic weight gain and bodily changes are due to a severe metabolic slowdown caused by chronic workplace stress.
concerns: She is worried that her growing muscle weakness will soon prevent her from climbing stairs and keeping up with her full-time job.
expectations: She hopes the doctor can run specific tests to explain why her body is changing so drastically and give her a treatment plan to reverse it.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Cushing's Disease (pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Cushing's Disease (pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes confirmatory biochemical testing (low-dose dexamethasone suppression, 24-hour urinary free cortisol) followed by pituitary MRI, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: facial puffiness, central weight gain, and purple stretch marks
Key HPI features: 39F with 1-year history of moon facies, buffalo hump, violaceous abdominal striae, and proximal weakness. Elevated 24h urinary cortisol.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 148/92, HR 80. Facial plethora, dorsocervical fat pad (buffalo hump), wide violaceous abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness. Bloods: 24-hour urinary free cortisol elevated; low-dose dexamethasone suppression test fails to suppress cortisol; Plasma ACTH normal/elevated (suggesting ACTH-dependent Cushing's).
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Cushing's Disease (pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adrenal Cushing's syndrome without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: New severe hypertension or psychiatric symptoms — part of the syndrome's systemic impact.
management_principles: Perform low-dose dexamethasone suppression test and 24-hour urinary free cortisol, then pituitary MRI with contrast
Refer to endocrinology and neurosurgery for potential transsphenoidal resection
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A pituitary tumor overproduces ACTH, driving excess cortisol and causing moon facies, a buffalo hump, violaceous striae, and proximal muscle weakness — confirmed by elevated 24-hour urinary cortisol.
red_flags: New severe hypertension or psychiatric symptoms — part of the syndrome's systemic impact

must_ask.say: Has the weight gain been mostly around your belly, with a rounder face?
Any purple stretch marks or easy bruising?
Is it hard to climb stairs or get up from a chair?
How long has this been developing?
Have you used any steroid medications?

history.answer: My face has become noticeably round and puffy, and I keep gaining weight around my belly while my arms and legs seem thinner. I've also noticed these wide, dark purple stretch marks on my stomach.
It started gradually about a year ago. It wasn't sudden; my face just slowly got rounder and the belly fat kept building up over several months.
The fat is gathering mostly around my face, the back of my neck, and my stomach. My arms and legs actually feel like they are shrinking and getting thinner.
I have these wide, dark purple stretch marks across my lower belly and flanks. My skin also feels paper-thin, and I get bruises from the slightest bump without remembering hitting anything.
Over the past year, it has steadily gotten worse. At first I thought it was just regular weight gain, but diet and exercise haven't stopped it at all.
Nothing I do seems to make it better. Eating less or exercising harder hasn't reduced the weight or changed how swollen my face looks.
I've been feeling so weak in my thighs and upper arms. It has become really hard to climb stairs or even stand up from a low chair without pushing off with my hands.
I feel tired all the time and have trouble sleeping through the night. My mood has also been really up and down, and I feel much more anxious and irritable than usual.
No, I haven't had any fevers, chills, or night sweats.
No, I don't have blurry vision, double vision, or loss of side vision. My headaches have only been occasional tension-type headaches, nothing severe.
No, I haven't had chest pain, shortness of breath, or heart racing.
No nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or constipation. My appetite has been slightly increased, but otherwise my digestion feels normal.
No, I've never experienced anything like this before in my life.
I tried strict dieting, cutting carbohydrates, and working out regularly, but none of it helped. I haven't taken any weight-loss pills or water pills.
No, I have never taken steroid pills, used steroid creams, or received cortisone joint injections. I've also never used steroid inhalers.
I haven't traveled anywhere, changed jobs, or had any unusual chemical or environmental exposures.
I've been wondering if extreme stress at work completely wrecked my metabolism and threw all my hormones out of whack.
I'm really worried because my legs are getting so weak that I'm struggling to climb the stairs at work, and I can't afford to lose my job.
I'm hoping you can run the right tests to explain what's happening to my body and give me a clear plan to get back to normal.
I have never had any chronic health conditions, and my blood pressure had always been normal at past checkups.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pain relievers, herbal remedies, or supplements.
No, I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
My periods have become very irregular and light over the past six months, and my last period was about six weeks ago.
My husband and I use barrier contraception consistently, and a home pregnancy test I took last week was negative.
My desire for sex has dropped completely over the past year, which is very unusual for me.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only have a glass of wine socially once or twice a month, and I don't drink liquor or beer.
I work full-time at an office desk job, and I live at home with my husband.
There is no family history of pituitary tumors, adrenal disorders, or early endocrine diseases.
It has really taken a toll on my self-confidence and daily routine. Just getting up from my desk or carrying groceries feels exhausting because of the weakness in my legs.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 148/92 mmHg, heart rate 80 beats per minute, afebrile, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Noticeable facial plethora, rounded moon facies, and prominent dorsocervical fat accumulation.
Visual fields are full to confrontation bilaterally; normal pupillary light reflexes and intact extraocular movements.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, with no palpable nodules or bruits.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Centripetal adiposity with prominent, wide violaceous striae across the lower abdomen; no surgical scars.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, non-distended, with no guarding, rigidity, or palpable masses.
Thin, fragile skin with wide purple striae on the abdomen and multiple scattered ecchymoses over the forearms.
Proximal muscle weakness in bilateral shoulder abductors and hip flexors (grade 4/5); distal muscle strength remains intact (grade 5/5).
Trace bilateral non-pitting edema over the ankles; calves are soft and non-tender without erythema.
